title: Overview and justification
body:
This short course is about making the most of practice and work-based learning: placements, laboratory and studio work, field work, simulations and projects. You already know what these are. The aim here is to turn an experience into real gains. By the end you will be able to identify what an experience can offer and set aims for it, apply practical strategies to get the most from it, and prepare for how it is assessed.

Practice and work-based learning is where your subject meets the working world. Tutors build it into more and more courses because employers value it, and because doing the work teaches things a lecture cannot. How much you gain, though, depends far less on the placement you land than on what you bring to it.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: identify what a practice or work-based experience can offer you and set clear aims for it
apply practical strategies to get the most out of a practice or work-based experience
prepare for how practice and work-based learning is assessed.

title: In real academic practice
body: Practice and work-based learning is where what you study meets what you will do. Every placement, laboratory session, field trip or project is a chance to build skills, judgement and contacts that your degree alone cannot give you. The habits in this course, aiming, acting and evidencing, are ones you will use in every such experience, and in the professional work that follows.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, what the experience offers: the benefits on the table and how to aim for them. Second, making the most of it: the moves that turn time served into value gained. Third, showing what you learned: how practice is assessed and how to evidence your learning. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, workplaces and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, placement or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Orientation
body: You are doing, or about to do, some practice or work-based learning: a placement, a lab or studio, field work, a simulation or a project. This lesson is about what such an experience can actually give you, and how to decide what you want from it before you start. Knowing that turns a requirement on your course into an opportunity you can steer.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You already know what practice and work-based learning is, so this lesson does not define it again. It assumes you will be in one of these settings soon, and focuses on the value you can draw out rather than on the basics of the setting itself.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: identify the main benefits a practice or work-based experience can offer you
recognise the difference between drifting through an experience and drawing value from it
set a clear aim for a practice or work-based experience in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Practice and work-based learning offers something a classroom cannot: authentic, real-world experience of the environment you intend to work in. That experience builds several things at once. It develops practical skills and professional judgement. It grows your employability and graduate capital, the know-how, networks and track record employers look for. And it feeds your personal development, showing you how you work and where you want to go.

These benefits are on offer, but they are not automatic. Two students can spend the same weeks on the same placement and leave with very different gains. What separates them is whether they knew what they were there to get, and aimed for it.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about a practice or work-based experience you have done or are about to do. What are two or three things you most want to get from it?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: A practice or work-based experience offers real skills, employability and self-knowledge, but only to the student who aims for them. You can now identify what such an experience can give you, recognise the difference between drifting and drawing value, and set clear aims of your own. The next lesson turns those aims into action: the moves that get the most out of the experience while you are in it.

title: Orientation
body: You have your aims. This lesson is about what to do with them once you are in the experience. Making the most of a placement or project is less about luck than about a handful of deliberate moves, made before you start, while you are there, and after you finish.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are past needing permission to take initiative. This lesson assumes you can act for yourself in a workplace or project, and focuses on which moves repay the effort most.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: apply practical strategies for getting the most out of a practice or work-based experience
distinguish a proactive approach to an experience from a passive one
choose an active move to make during a practice or work-based experience in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Getting the most out of an experience comes down to being proactive across three phases. Before you start, prepare: set your aims, find out about the setting, and arrange who will support you. While you are there, engage: volunteer for tasks, ask questions, watch how skilled people work, and seek feedback rather than waiting for it. After you finish, consolidate: record what you did, reflect on what you learned, and connect it to your development and your CV.

The thread through all three is initiative. The experience rarely hands you its value; you take it, through the questions you ask and the chances you put yourself forward for.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about a time you took part in something without taking much initiative. What is one proactive move you could make next time?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: You get the most out of an experience by being proactive across three phases: preparing and aiming before, taking initiative and seeking feedback during, and recording and connecting afterwards. You can now apply these strategies, tell a proactive approach from a passive one, and choose an active move when you are in the thick of it. The last lesson is about showing what all this produced: how practice is assessed, and how to evidence your learning.

title: Orientation
body: The work is only half the task. Most practice and work-based learning is assessed, and the assessment rarely marks the work itself. It marks what you can show you learned from it. This lesson is about how that assessment tends to work, and how to give it strong evidence.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You have met assessment before, so this lesson does not explain marks and feedback from scratch. It focuses on what is distinctive about assessing an experience, where the grade comes from something you cannot simply revise for.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain how practice and work-based learning is typically assessed and why standardised criteria are difficult
tell strong evidence of learning apart from a bare description of what happened
prepare evidence for how a practice or work-based experience in {{context}} is assessed.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Practice and work-based learning is hard to assess with a standard exam. Every workplace has its own culture and tasks, so tutors cannot set one fixed test for all. Instead they assess what you can show you learned, usually through reflective accounts, portfolios, reports or presentations. The grade comes from the quality of your evidence, not from how busy your placement looked.

That makes one distinction decisive: evidence versus description. Describing what happened, the tasks, the days, the people, earns little on its own. Strong evidence goes further: it shows what you learned, points to something specific that happened, and says what you would do with that learning. Keeping a record as you go is what makes such evidence possible.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about an experience you could be asked to write up. Which one or two moments actually taught you something?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Practice and work-based learning is assessed on the learning you can show, not on the activity itself, which is why evidence beats description. You can now explain how the assessment works and why standard criteria are hard, tell evidence apart from description, and prepare strong evidence of your own. With aims set, the experience worked actively, and your learning evidenced, you are ready to make the most of whatever practice your course brings.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Making the most of practice and work-based learning is now something you can plan rather than hope for. You can identify what an experience offers and set aims to steer it. You can apply the moves, preparing, taking initiative, seeking feedback and recording, that turn time into learning. And you can meet the assessment by showing evidence of what you learned, not just an account of what you did. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, every placement, project, laboratory or field experience your course brings is a chance to put this to work. Aim, act and evidence, and the same experience gives you more. These are also the habits professional life rewards: people who get the most from what they do, and can show for it, are the ones who progress.

title: Where this goes next
body: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the advanced course takes experience into structured reflection, using Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle to turn what happened into insight you can articulate. Going wider: Reflective Practice, Understanding Learning, Assessment and Feedback, and Presenting all draw on the same habits of learning by doing and showing what you gained.

title: Explore the concept
body: Three things a practice or work-based experience can build for you. Review each card to see what it offers.
instruction: Read through the cards below.

_items.title: Real-world skills
_items.subtitle: What you can do
_items.text: A practice setting lets you do the work, not just read about it: using the equipment, handling the cases, running the process. You build skills employers recognise because you have actually done them.

_items.title: Employability and capital
_items.subtitle: What you can show
_items.text: An experience grows your graduate capital: the know-how, contacts and track record that make you employable. A placement you can talk about with specifics is worth far more than a line on a CV.

_items.title: Personal development
_items.subtitle: What you learn about yourself
_items.text: Doing real work shows you how you think, where you are strong, and what you want from a career. That self-knowledge shapes the choices you make next.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students take up the same month-long placement.

{{learner-a}} turns up each day, does what is asked, and goes home. The tasks get done. But {{learner-a}} never decided what the placement was for, so it drifts: no goal to steer by, no sense of what to notice, nothing gathered beyond the hours served. At the end there is little to show but attendance.

{{learner-b}} starts the same placement with two or three clear aims: to learn one technical skill, to understand how the team makes decisions, and to leave with examples for a CV. Those aims shape each day, what to volunteer for, what to ask, what to note. The same month yields skills, insight and evidence.

Both served the same time. Only {{learner-b}} decided in advance what to draw from it, and so actually drew it.

title: Setting your aims
body: These questions turn a vague sense of wanting to do well into clear aims you can steer by. Use them before your next experience.
instruction: Tick each item once you have thought it through.

_items.text: Have I written down two or three things I want from this experience?
Does at least one aim name a skill I want to build?
Does one aim concern how the workplace or team actually works?
Have I thought about what evidence I want to leave with?
Have I checked my aims against what the assessment asks for?
Have I shared my aims with my supervisor or tutor so they can help?

title: Formative check: what an experience offers
displayTitle: Which of these best describes what a practice or work-based experience mainly offers you?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which best describes what a practice or work-based experience mainly offers you?

_items.text: A chance to build real skills, employability and self-knowledge by doing the work.
_items.feedback: Yes. Doing the work builds skills, capital and self-knowledge at once.

_items.text: A guaranteed job offer at the end of the placement.
_items.feedback: An experience builds employability, but it does not guarantee a job.

_items.text: A lighter workload than the taught part of your course.
_items.feedback: Practice learning is not an easier option; it asks a different kind of effort.

_items.text: A set of notes you can revise from for an exam.
_items.feedback: Its value is in doing and learning, not in revision notes.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A practice or work-based experience builds real skills, employability and self-knowledge through doing the work.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what doing real work gives you that a classroom cannot.
_incorrect.final: An experience mainly offers the chance to build skills, employability and self-knowledge by doing the work, not a guaranteed job, an easier load or revision notes.

title: Formative check: drifting versus drawing value
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's month more valuable than the first's?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's month more valuable?

_items.text: They set clear aims in advance, which shaped what they did, asked and gathered.
_items.feedback: Yes. Clear aims steered the whole month.

_items.text: They were given more interesting tasks than the first student.
_items.feedback: Both took up the same placement; the tasks were not the difference.

_items.text: They spent more hours on the placement than the first student.
_items.feedback: Both served the same time; what differed was the aim they brought.

_items.text: They were naturally more confident than the first student.
_items.feedback: The difference was deciding what to draw from it, not personality.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student set aims in advance, and those aims shaped what they did, asked and gathered.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second student decided before the placement began.
_incorrect.final: The second student's month was more valuable because they set clear aims in advance, which steered what they did, asked and gathered, not because of better tasks, more hours or confidence.

title: Formative check: setting an aim
displayTitle: You are about to start a practice or work-based experience in {{context}}. Which is the best way to set a clear aim for it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which is the best way to set a clear aim for an experience?

_items.text: Name two or three specific things to gain, a skill, an insight, some evidence, and let them steer your days.
_items.feedback: Yes. Specific aims in {{context}} give you something to steer by.

_items.text: Decide to work hard and see what comes up.
_items.feedback: Working hard without an aim leaves the experience to drift.

_items.text: Wait until the end to see what you happened to learn.
_items.feedback: Leaving it to the end means nothing steered the time in between.

_items.text: Aim simply to complete the required hours.
_items.feedback: Hours served is attendance, not a learning aim.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, a clear aim names two or three specific gains and lets them steer your days.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that names specific gains in advance.
_incorrect.final: A clear aim in {{context}} names two or three specific things to gain and uses them to steer each day, rather than trusting hard work, hindsight or hours served.

title: Explore the concept
body: The moves that get the most out of an experience fall into three phases. Reveal each one to see the move it asks for.
instruction: Select each stage to reveal the move it describes.

_items.title: Prepare and aim
_items.body: Set two or three aims, find out what the setting does, and agree with your supervisor how they can help. You arrive ready to steer, not just to turn up.

_items.title: Take the initiative
_items.body: Volunteer for tasks that stretch you, ask how and why decisions are made, and watch skilled people closely. The chances you put yourself forward for are the ones you learn from.

_items.title: Seek feedback
_items.body: Do not wait for an end-of-placement review. Ask how a task went while it is fresh, and act on what you hear. Feedback sought early changes what you do next.

_items.title: Record and connect
_items.body: Write down what you did and learned while you remember it, and connect each gain to your development and your CV. Value you cannot recall is value lost.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students spend a term on the same research project placement.

{{learner-a}} waits to be given jobs and does them well enough. When a task is unclear, {{learner-a}} guesses rather than asks, and never requests feedback for fear of seeming unsure. The work passes, but no one stretches {{learner-a}}, and the placement ends much as it began.

{{learner-b}} asks, on the first day, what would make the term useful to the team, and volunteers for a task just beyond current skill. When something is unclear, {{learner-b}} checks early; after each piece of work, {{learner-b}} asks what could be stronger. By the end, {{learner-b}} has done harder work, learned faster, and is remembered.

Same project, same length. {{learner-b}} took the initiative that turned time into learning.

title: Active moves
body: These moves turn time served into learning gained. Try them during your next experience.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I volunteered for at least one task that stretches me?
When something was unclear, did I ask rather than guess?
Have I asked for feedback on a task while it was still fresh?
Have I watched how an experienced person handles the work?
Have I recorded what I did and learned, soon after doing it?
Have I connected a gain from this week to one of my aims?

title: Formative check: getting the most out of it
displayTitle: Which set of actions is most likely to get the most out of a practice or work-based experience?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which set of actions gets the most out of an experience?

_items.text: Preparing aims beforehand, taking initiative and seeking feedback during, and recording learning afterwards.
_items.feedback: Yes. Being proactive across all three phases is the key.

_items.text: Waiting to be told what to do and doing it carefully.
_items.feedback: Careful compliance alone leaves most of the value untaken.

_items.text: Keeping your head down and avoiding mistakes.
_items.feedback: Avoiding risk also avoids the tasks you would learn most from.

_items.text: Doing the minimum needed to pass the assessment.
_items.feedback: The minimum earns a pass but wastes the experience.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Preparing, taking initiative, seeking feedback and recording are the moves that get the most from an experience.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that is proactive before, during and after.
_incorrect.final: Getting the most out of an experience means preparing aims, taking initiative and seeking feedback during, and recording afterwards, not waiting, playing safe or doing the minimum.

title: Formative check: proactive versus passive
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's term more productive than the first's?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's term more productive?

_items.text: They took the initiative: asking, volunteering for stretch, and seeking feedback early.
_items.feedback: Yes. Initiative turned the same term into more learning.

_items.text: They were given easier tasks that were simpler to complete.
_items.feedback: They took on harder work, not easier.

_items.text: They avoided asking questions so as not to seem unsure.
_items.feedback: That describes the first student, who guessed rather than asked.

_items.text: They waited to be told exactly what to do at each step.
_items.feedback: Waiting to be told is the passive approach, not the productive one.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student took the initiative, asking, volunteering and seeking feedback, which turned the term into learning.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second student did rather than waited for.
_incorrect.final: The second student's term was more productive because they took the initiative: asking, volunteering for stretch and seeking feedback early, rather than waiting, playing safe or guessing.

title: Formative check: an active move
displayTitle: You are partway through a practice or work-based experience in {{context}} and a task is unclear. Which is the active move this lesson recommends?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which is the active move when a task is unclear?

_items.text: Ask early how it should be done, then act on the answer.
_items.feedback: Yes. Checking early is the active move in {{context}}.

_items.text: Guess, and hope it turns out to be right.
_items.feedback: Guessing risks the work and teaches you nothing reliable.

_items.text: Do nothing until someone notices and explains.
_items.feedback: Waiting to be rescued wastes the chance to learn by asking.

_items.text: Leave that task and pick an easier one instead.
_items.feedback: Avoiding the task avoids the learning in it.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, the active move is to ask early and then act on the answer.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that seeks the answer rather than avoiding the task.
_incorrect.final: The active move in {{context}} is to ask early how a task should be done and then act on the answer, rather than guessing, waiting or avoiding it.

title: Explore the concept
body: Four things to understand about how practice and work-based learning is assessed. Reveal each in turn.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all four.

_items.title: Why there is no standard test
_items.body: Each setting has its own culture and tasks, so a single fixed exam would not fit them all. Tutors assess your learning from the experience instead of the experience itself.

_items.title: What the evidence looks like
_items.body: Reflective accounts, portfolios, reports and presentations are the usual forms. Each asks you to show learning, not just to report activity.

_items.title: Description versus evidence
_items.body: Saying what you did is description. Showing what you learned, with a specific example and what you will do with it, is evidence. The marks follow the evidence.

_items.title: Why you record as you go
_items.body: Strong evidence rests on specifics you will not remember weeks later. A running note of what happened and what you learned is what makes a good account possible.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students write up the same hospital placement for assessment.

{{learner-a}} describes the weeks in order: the wards visited, the staff met, the tasks observed. It is accurate and complete, and it reads like a diary. But it stays at the level of what happened, so a marker learns what {{learner-a}} did without learning what {{learner-a}} took from it.

{{learner-b}} picks a few moments that taught something and builds on each. One handover showed how a team shares risk; {{learner-b}} explains what that revealed about communication and how it will change their own practice. The account is shorter on events but rich in learning.

Both did the same placement. {{learner-b}} offered evidence of learning, where {{learner-a}} offered only a record of activity.

title: Building your evidence
body: These questions turn a record of activity into evidence of learning. Use them as you prepare an assessed account.
instruction: Tick each item once you have checked it.

_items.text: Have I checked what form the assessment takes and what it rewards?
Am I keeping a running note of what happens and what I learn?
For each point, have I shown learning rather than just reporting activity?
Have I tied a specific moment to each thing I claim to have learned?
Have I said what I would do differently or next as a result?
Have I chosen a few strong examples rather than listing everything?

title: Formative check: how it is assessed
displayTitle: Why do tutors usually assess practice and work-based learning through reflective accounts or portfolios rather than a standard exam?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is practice learning assessed by account or portfolio rather than an exam?

_items.text: Each setting differs, so they assess the learning you can show rather than the experience itself.
_items.feedback: Yes. Settings vary too much for one fixed test.

_items.text: Exams are simply going out of fashion across the university.
_items.feedback: The reason is the variety of settings, not fashion.

_items.text: Reflective accounts are quicker for tutors to mark.
_items.feedback: Ease of marking is not the reason; it is the variety of settings.

_items.text: Because practice learning does not really need assessing.
_items.feedback: It is assessed; the question is how, given how settings differ.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Settings differ too much for one standard test, so tutors assess the learning you can show.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about why one fixed exam would not fit every placement.
_incorrect.final: Practice learning is assessed by account or portfolio because each setting differs, so tutors assess the learning you can show rather than the experience itself.

title: Formative check: evidence versus description
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's write-up stronger evidence than the first's?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's write-up stronger evidence?

_items.text: It showed what was learned from specific moments and what would change, rather than listing what happened.
_items.feedback: Yes. Learning tied to specifics is evidence.

_items.text: It covered more of the weeks in greater detail.
_items.feedback: More coverage is fuller description, not stronger evidence.

_items.text: It was written more neatly and with fewer errors.
_items.feedback: Presentation is not what turns description into evidence.

_items.text: It quoted the supervisor's praise of the placement.
_items.feedback: Praise is not evidence of what the student learned.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Showing learning from specific moments, and what would change, is what makes it evidence.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second student showed beyond what happened.
_incorrect.final: The second write-up was stronger evidence because it showed learning from specific moments and what would change, rather than listing events, polishing the prose or quoting praise.

title: Formative check: preparing evidence
displayTitle: You are preparing an assessed account of a practice or work-based experience in {{context}}. Which approach gives the strongest evidence?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which approach gives the strongest evidence in an assessed account?

_items.text: Choose a few moments that taught you something, and for each show the learning and what you will do with it.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, learning tied to specific moments is the strongest evidence.

_items.text: Describe every week in order so nothing is left out.
_items.feedback: A complete diary is description, not evidence of learning.

_items.text: List all the tasks you completed during the placement.
_items.feedback: A task list reports activity; it does not show learning.

_items.text: Focus on how many hours you put in.
_items.feedback: Hours show effort, not what you learned.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, the strongest evidence shows learning from a few specific moments and what you will do with it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that shows learning rather than reporting activity.
_incorrect.final: The strongest evidence in {{context}} chooses a few telling moments and, for each, shows the learning and what you will do with it, rather than describing every week, listing tasks or counting hours.

ariaQuestion: A practice or work-based experience mainly offers the chance to...

_items.text: build real skills, employability and self-knowledge by doing the work.
_items.feedback: Yes. Doing the work builds skills, capital and self-knowledge.

_items.text: avoid the harder taught parts of your course.
_items.feedback: It is not an easier option; it asks a different kind of effort.

_items.text: secure a guaranteed job at the end.
_items.feedback: It builds employability but guarantees nothing.

_items.text: gather notes to revise from for an exam.
_items.feedback: Its value is in doing and learning, not revision notes.

_feedback.correct: That's right. An experience mainly offers skills, employability and self-knowledge gained by doing the work.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what doing real work gives you.

body: What most determines how much a student gains from a placement?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What most determines how much a student gains from a placement?

_items.text: What they aim for and bring to it, more than which placement it is.
_items.feedback: Yes. The aim you bring matters more than the placement itself.

_items.text: How prestigious the host organisation is.
_items.feedback: Prestige does not decide what you take from it.

_items.text: How many hours the placement lasts.
_items.feedback: Hours served is attendance, not gain.

_items.text: How closely it matches the lectures already given.
_items.feedback: The gain comes from what you aim for, not from matching lectures.

_feedback.correct: That's right. What a student aims for and brings to a placement matters more than which placement it is.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what separated the two students in the first lesson.

body: Which of these best describes a proactive approach to a work-based experience?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which best describes a proactive approach to a work-based experience?

_items.text: Volunteering for stretching tasks, asking when unclear, and seeking feedback early.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is initiative across the experience.

_items.text: Waiting to be told what to do and doing it carefully.
_items.feedback: Careful compliance is passive, not proactive.

_items.text: Avoiding questions so as not to seem unsure.
_items.feedback: Avoiding questions is the passive approach.

_items.text: Keeping your head down to avoid any mistakes.
_items.feedback: Playing safe avoids the tasks you learn most from.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Volunteering, asking and seeking feedback early is the proactive approach.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that takes initiative.

body: After finishing a placement, which move best secures its value?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: After a placement, which move best secures its value?

_items.text: Recording what you did and learned, and connecting it to your development.
_items.feedback: Yes. Recording and connecting keeps the value you gained.

_items.text: Putting it out of mind until results arrive.
_items.feedback: Value you do not record is easily lost.

_items.text: Starting the next thing straight away without review.
_items.feedback: Without review, the learning fades unrecorded.

_items.text: Listing the hours you completed for your records.
_items.feedback: Hours are attendance, not the learning to secure.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Recording what you learned and connecting it to your development secures the value.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about the 'after' phase in the second lesson.

body: Why is practice and work-based learning usually assessed by portfolio or reflective account rather than a fixed exam?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is practice learning assessed by portfolio rather than a fixed exam?

_items.text: Settings differ too much for one standard test, so the learning you can show is assessed.
_items.feedback: Yes. Variety of settings is the reason.

_items.text: Exams are being phased out across higher education.
_items.feedback: The reason is the variety of settings, not phasing out.

_items.text: Portfolios are always quicker to mark.
_items.feedback: Ease of marking is not the reason.

_items.text: Practice learning does not really need assessing.
_items.feedback: It is assessed; the question is how.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Settings vary too much for one fixed test, so the learning you can show is assessed.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about why one exam could not fit every placement.

body: Which turns a description of a placement into strong evidence of learning?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which turns a description into strong evidence of learning?

_items.text: Showing what specific moments taught you and what you will do with it.
_items.feedback: Yes. Learning tied to specifics is evidence.

_items.text: Describing every week in careful order.
_items.feedback: That is fuller description, not evidence.

_items.text: Listing all the tasks you completed.
_items.feedback: A task list reports activity, not learning.

_items.text: Stating how many hours the placement took.
_items.feedback: Hours show effort, not learning.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Showing what specific moments taught you, and what you will do with it, is strong evidence.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about the difference between description and evidence.

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: what an experience can offer and how to aim for it, the proactive moves that get the most from it, and how to evidence what you learned. On their own they are three separate ideas. This lesson brings them together into one practice you can run every time.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are not expected to have this down to a routine. The aim is to see aiming, acting and evidencing as one practice rather than three separate ideas, so that it carries on past this course into every experience your studies bring.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: connect setting aims, acting proactively and evidencing your learning into one practice for any experience
analyse how this practice works across a student's run of placements and projects
apply the three together to keep making the most of practice or work-based experiences in {{context}} beyond this course

title: Concept: definition
body: Making the most of experience is one practice, not three separate lessons. You run the same loop for every placement or project: aim for what you want, act to get it, and evidence what you learned. The three ideas from the earlier lessons are the parts of that single practice. You can repeat it every time, carrying each lesson into the next experience.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, this becomes one habit you run for every placement, project or lab, not a one-off effort. Before each experience you set a few clear aims; while you are there you act on them and seek feedback; afterwards you evidence what you learned. The best part is carrying one lesson into how you aim next time. Over a course, those rounds build real skill and a record to show for it.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about a practice or work-based experience coming up in your studies. How will you aim, act and evidence on it, and carry what you learn into the next one?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Making the most of experience is most powerful when it becomes one continuing practice. You aim, act and evidence, again and again, and carry each lesson into the next experience. It is the practice, not any single placement, that builds your skill and your record over time.

title: Lesson Sources
instruction: This lesson draws on the following sources.

_items.title: See pages 42 to 43 of Chapter 3 of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).
See pages 73 to 74 of Chapter 5 of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).
See pages 93 to 94 of Chapter 6 of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: The practice as one cycle
body: The same loop runs for every placement or project, not three separate tasks. Select each part to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each part of the cycle.

_items.title: Aim
_items.body: Set two or three clear aims before the experience begins, so you know what you want from it.

_items.title: Act
_items.body: Act on those aims while you are there, taking the initiative and seeking feedback as you go.

_items.title: Evidence
_items.body: Evidence what you learned, with specific examples, when the experience is assessed.

_items.title: Carry forward
_items.body: Carry what you learned into how you aim for the next experience, then run the loop again.

_diagram.title: Making the most of experience as a continuing loop

title: Worked example
body: Two students take a series of placements over their course. One treats each as a fresh start: no aims, little initiative, and a write-up that just lists what happened. The other runs the same practice every time, aiming, acting and evidencing, and uses what each placement teaches to aim better on the next. By the final placement, the second student is doing harder work and can show exactly what they gained.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: Checklist: How to keep making the most of it
body: Use these to keep the practice running across every experience, rather than starting each one from scratch.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Did I set clear aims before this experience, not just turn up?
Did I act on those aims, taking initiative and seeking feedback?
Did I keep a record I can turn into evidence of learning?
Did I show what I learned, not just what I did?
Did I carry one lesson into how I approach the next experience?

displayTitle: Why is it better to treat aiming, acting and evidencing as one practice rather than three separate tasks?
body: Why is it better to treat aiming, acting and evidencing as one practice rather than three separate tasks?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it better to treat aiming, acting and evidencing as one practice rather than three separate tasks?

_items.text: Because they feed one another: clear aims shape how you act, and acting well gives you something real to evidence.
_items.feedback: Yes. Each part sets up the next, so running them together gets more from the experience.

_items.text: Because doing all three once, in detail, fixes how you learn for good.
_items.feedback: One pass rarely changes a habit. The practice works when you repeat it for each experience.

_items.text: Because treating them as one means you can skip the evidence at the end.
_items.feedback: Evidence is part of the practice, not a step you drop. It is where the learning is shown.

_items.text: Because one practice takes less effort than aiming, acting and evidencing.
_items.feedback: It is not about less effort. One connected practice spreads the effort and makes each part count.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Run together, aiming, acting and evidencing feed one another, so you get more from every experience.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what you gain by connecting the three parts rather than doing each one alone.

displayTitle: A student sets aims for a placement, takes initiative and seeks feedback throughout, then evidences what they learned. They carry one lesson into their next placement, which goes better. What does this show?
body: A student sets aims for a placement, takes initiative and seeks feedback throughout, then evidences what they learned. They carry one lesson into their next placement, which goes better. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student sets aims for a placement, takes initiative and seeks feedback throughout, then evidences what they learned. They carry one lesson into their next placement, which goes better. What does this show?

_items.text: That making the most of experience works as one continuing practice, run across placement after placement.
_items.feedback: Yes. The whole loop ran, and carrying it forward improved the next placement.

_items.text: That the first placement was a better opportunity than most.
_items.feedback: The point is not the placement itself. It is the practice the student ran on it.

_items.text: That evidencing learning is the only part that matters.
_items.feedback: Evidencing is one part. Aiming and acting came first and made the evidence possible.

_items.text: That this only works for students who are naturally confident.
_items.feedback: The practice helped this student whatever their starting point. It is the habit, not the personality.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Aim, act, evidence, then carry a lesson forward: that is the practice running across experiences.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at what the student did across the two placements, not just one.

displayTitle: You want to make the most of your next practice or work-based experience in {{context}}. Which plan best treats aiming, acting and evidencing as one continuing practice?
body: You want to make the most of your next practice or work-based experience in {{context}}. Which plan best treats aiming, acting and evidencing as one continuing practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to make the most of your next practice or work-based experience in your subject. Which plan best treats aiming, acting and evidencing as one continuing practice?

_items.text: Set clear aims before you start, act on them and seek feedback throughout, then evidence what you learned and carry a lesson into the next experience.
_items.feedback: Yes. That runs the whole practice in {{context}}, and keeps it going.

_items.text: Wait until the experience is over, then write up everything at once.
_items.feedback: Leaving it all to the end means nothing steered the experience while it ran.

_items.text: Only act when you are told to, so you avoid getting things wrong.
_items.feedback: Waiting to be told leaves most of the value untaken. The practice needs initiative.

_items.text: Aim and act, but skip evidencing to save time at the end.
_items.feedback: Evidencing is where the learning is shown. Dropping it loses the proof of what you gained.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Aiming, acting, evidencing and carrying a lesson forward keeps the practice going in {{context}}.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the plan that runs all three parts and repeats them over time.
